phonemes.desc: Long ā as in “father”; the name is reconstructed Proto-Celtic *Dānu.
The final u is long; the name descends from the Indo-European river-mother *dānu, “the flowing one”.
The eponym of the Tuatha Dé Danann — “the peoples of the goddess Danu”.

kin.label: River family
kin.form: Danube, Don, Dnieper, Dysna — all from the same *dānu root

kin.label: Eponym
kin.form: the Tuatha Dé Danann, “the peoples of Danu”

pronunciation.note: The name is the same word as the Danube and the Don — the river-mother of the Indo-Europeans, eponym of Ireland’s divine race.

domains.title: Knowledge, Wisdom, Mother of the Tuatha Dé Danann
domains.subtitle: The River-Mother of the Divine Race
domains.lead: Danu is Ireland’s primordial mother-goddess: the eponym of the Tuatha Dé Danann, the ‘peoples of Danu’, the divine race who came from the northern islands to take Ireland in the island’s deepest legends. She herself barely appears in the texts — her children take every scene — but the race’s name keeps hers, and the river-name she shares with the Danube and the Don marks her as the Celtic river-mother, the flowing one beneath the whole family.

mythology.lead: Danu’s mythology is peculiar: she is everywhere in the name and nowhere in the stories. The Tuatha Dé Danann — her peoples — fill the Mythological Cycle’s battles and sorceries, but their mother never takes the stage. Her biography is her children’s: the coming from the northern islands, the four treasures, the battles of Mag Tuired, and the fading into the sídhe, the hollow hills where the divine race retired when the sons of Míl took Ireland.

myths.title: The Peoples of Danu Arrive
myths.text: The Book of Invasions tells it as history: the Tuatha Dé Danann came from the northern islands in dark clouds, burned their ships behind them on the Irish shore, and contended for the island against the Fir Bolg and the Fomoiri. From each of the four cities they brought a treasure — the stone of Fál, the spear of Lugh, the sword of Nuadu, the cauldron of the Dagda — the four regalia of the divine race, each a gift of Danu’s line.

myths.title: The Battles of Mag Tuired
myths.text: The race’s great war-cycle pits them against the Fomoiri, the sea-demons of chaos: Nuadu’s silver arm, Lugh’s many skills, the Dagda’s bottomless cauldron, and the Morrígan’s prophecy carry the day. Danu’s name stands over the whole cycle — the mother’s eponym on every battle-line, though she herself never draws a sword in the telling.

myths.title: The Retirement into the Hills
myths.text: When the sons of Míl defeated the Dé Danann, the race did not die but withdrew — into the sídhe, the hollow hills of Ireland, where they keep their beauty and their treasure and their grievance, and from where they still interfere, bless, and curse. Danu’s peoples became the fairies of Irish tradition; their mother’s name contracted into the fairy-mounds’ oldest title.

myths.title: The Danube’s Sister
myths.text: The philology is the mythology here: *dānu, ‘the flowing one’, names rivers from the Danube to the Don to the Dnieper — the Indo-European river-mother’s name scattered across the map like water-systems. Irish Danu is the westernmost daughter of the family; her son the Dagda’s name has been read as ‘the good god’, the river’s generous flood made divine.

lore.syncretism: Danu is the Celtic branch of the Indo-European river-mother — kin to the Vedic Danu, mother of the demon Vṛtra in the Rigveda’s oldest combat, across the very language-family the names share. The Tuatha Dé Danann were euhemerized by the medieval Irish scholars into a people of sorcerers; the modern Celtic revival restored them to goddess-worship, with Danu as the primordial name.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her name survives in the Tuatha Dé Danann’s — the divine race of every Irish legend of consequence — and in the river-network of Europe, the Danube most of all. The modern Druidic and Celtic-revival movements take Danu as the mother-goddess of their pantheon; and the sídhe-tradition she eponymizes is the ancestor of the world’s entire fairy-canon.
lore.extendedMeditation: Danu: the river-mother whose name flows through six European languages before it reaches this page. Restored plainly, it is the same word the Danube still spells with two syllables — the flowing one, the mother of a divine race, the water beneath the whole map.

sources.name: Lebor Gabála Érenn (the Book of Invasions)
Cath Maige Tuired (the Battles of Mag Tuired)

lore.archaeology: Danu leaves no image — the medieval manuscripts give her no body. But the sídhe-hills of Ireland (Teamhair, Brú na Bóinne) are her race’s palaces, and the river-names across Europe are her signature.
lore.cult: The modern Celtic revival keeps her cult — the seasonal gatherings and the mother-goddess invocations. The medieval tradition venerated her line at the sídhe-mounds; the fairy-legend itself is her oldest surviving liturgy.
lore.iconography: The river in flood, or the mother with the four treasures; in modern Druidic art, the flowing woman whose hair is the river-system. Her icon is the eponym itself — the race’s name, read backwards into the goddess.
lore.reception: Comparative mythology’s river-mother paradigm runs from the Vedic Danu to the Celtic one — the same *dānu across the Indo-European world. Celtic studies treat her as the supreme example of the eponymous goddess: the mother known only through her children’s fame.
